a27.speaker: Blade Nzimande, South Africa's Minister of Science, Technology and Innovation
a27.speech: Hailed the new pan-African Pharmaceutical Manufacturing Plan as a "truly historic development"; said the plan aims to ensure at least 60% of vaccines used in Africa are produced within Africa by 2040, with 10% of the continent's vaccine needs met locally by the end of this year. "It is about more than new facilities or technology transfers, it is an integrated ambition — to equip Africa's people, scientists, and manufacturers with the tools and skills to secure the continent's health sovereignty." Said the plan centres on expanding manufacturing capacity through regional hubs, implementing WHO-quality standards, and improving drug regulation through the African Medicines Agency. "Our challenge and obligation as policymakers, researchers, and industrialists is to turn these plans into performance, and these ambitions into real changes in the lives of the people we serve."

a27.speaker: Cyril Xaba, Mayor of eThekwini Municipality
a27.speech: Said the conference was taking place against the backdrop of "unprecedented retrenchment in aid spending," warning this is leading to deep cuts and restructuring across the global health landscape with immediate consequences for vital health programmes. "This is a crisis different to anything that has preceded it." "Yet it also presents us all with an opportunity to create a new system that not only better serves the priorities and aspirations of African countries, but also delivers a health security and prosperity dividend for the African region."

a27.speaker: OECD (Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development), report cited
a27.speech: Bilateral overseas development aid for countries in sub-Saharan Africa is projected to decline by between 16% and 28% this year, following a two per cent decline in 2024; overseas development aid for health could fall to levels not seen since the mid-2000s.

a27.speaker: Jean Kaseya, Director-General of Africa CDC
a27.speech: Said the continent's evolving role in health means that "for the first time, Africa is inspiring the world." "The world is learning from Africa." "This reform of global architecture means we are co-architects. We are 1.4 billion proud Africans making our own agenda. We are proud of that."

a27.speaker: Nhlanhla Msomi, President of AfricaBio
a27.speech: Underscored the urgency of building innovation capacity: "We know that our healthcare industry on the continent at large is using borrowed technologies, borrowed ideas, and borrowed science." "Unless we move away and decouple from that, we're not likely to win this battle."

a187.speaker: Myanmar military junta
a187.speech: Said today that the number of deaths caused by the earthquake that struck Myanmar on Friday has risen to more than 1,700. The previous toll, also given by the military junta, pointed to 1,644 dead, 3,408 injured and 139 missing.

a187.speaker: Major-General Zaw Min Tun, spokesman for the junta-controlled Government of Myanmar
a187.speech: Told the Burmese state broadcaster MRTV that another 3,400 people were injured and more than 300 are still missing.

a187.speaker: Local authorities in Bangkok, Thailand
a187.speech: According to the most recent toll from local authorities, released on Sunday, at least 18 people died, another 33 were injured and 78 are missing in Bangkok.

a187.speaker: Yoshimasa Hayashi, Japanese government spokesman
a187.speech: Said today at a press conference that the five-member team, made up of officials of the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) and medical personnel, will travel to the affected area to monitor the needs of the victims and the security situation on the ground.

a187.speaker: China International Development Cooperation Agency (cited by Lusa)
a187.speech: According to the agency, China sent to Myanmar the first batch of humanitarian aid, which includes tents, blankets and first aid equipment.

a187.speaker: World Health Organization (WHO)
a187.speech: On Sunday, the WHO classified the earthquake in Myanmar at the highest level of emergency and launched an urgent appeal to raise eight million dollars to save lives and prevent epidemics.

a518.speaker: National Ministry of Health of South Sudan (statement)
a518.speech: According to the ministry's statement, the new PHEOC launched on April 3 was established with support from the World Health Organization (WHO) and the US Agency for International Development (USAID).

a518.speaker: Dr. Annin Ngot Ngot, Undersecretary of the National Ministry of Health
a518.speech: Said the health unit is aimed to protect communities from health threats and enable responses to outbreaks and disasters.

a518.speaker: Dr. Kediende Chong Mapuor, Director General of Preventive Health Services and Emergencies Response
a518.speech: Emphasized the importance of collaboration among stakeholders for the centre's success.

a977.speaker: Wamkele Mene, Secretary General of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA)
a977.speech: Said the visit was to express his sincere appreciation to Dr. Bawumia for the support extended to the AfCFTA Secretariat during his tenure as Vice President of Ghana. “His Excellency, I am here today to express my sincere gratitude for the support you extended to the AfCFTA Secretariat during your tenure as the Vice President of the Republic.”

a977.speaker: Wamkele Mene, Secretary General of the AfCFTA
a977.speech: Commended Dr. Bawumia on his remarkable concession during the recently held presidential and parliamentary elections: “Ghana’s democratic credentials were further strengthened when you conceded defeat less than 24 hours after the presidential elections. You have indeed shown that you love your country and its people.”

a977.speaker: AfCFTA
a977.speech: Used the occasion to encourage Dr. Mahamudu Bawumia not to stop giving out his best in ensuring that the country moves forward.

a1179.speaker: Council of Ministers of Benin (extraordinary session communique of 29 March 2016)
a1179.speech: The Council of Ministers, meeting in extraordinary session on Tuesday 29 March 2016 chaired by the President of the Republic, was largely devoted to the summarised points of the government's achievements in the ministries since 2006, reporting that the macroeconomic framework remained broadly stable over the period 2006-2015, characterised by rapid economic growth, contained inflation, a controlled public deficit and efforts to consolidate and modernise public finances, with an average growth rate of 4.2%, inflation held at 2.7%, State revenue rising from 383.4 billion CFA francs in 2005 to 819.5 billion in 2015, and public debt sustainable at about 41.7% at end-December 2015.

a1179.speaker: Minister of State in charge of Public Works and Transport of Benin
a1179.speech: The review of achievements he presented shows that the road network evolved from a length of 1,821 km in 2006 to about 2,800 km in 2016, an increase of 1,000 km for an investment of more than 850 billion CFA francs, corresponding on average to 100 km per year in terms of rehabilitation, modernisation and extension; the review also covered road safety and rail and air transport.

a1179.speaker: BCEAO (Central Bank of West African States) (figures)
a1179.speech: According to the BCEAO figures, the investment rate would stand at 29%, compared with 16.5% in 2005.

a1179.speaker: United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) (2015 World Investment Report, published 24 June 2015)
a1179.speech: According to the report, Benin benefited during 2014 from incoming foreign direct investment of $377 million, about 226 billion CFA francs; these new UNCTAD data make the Beninese economy the 3rd most attractive economy of WAEMU for foreign capital and the 8th in West Africa, whereas it was the 6th destination of WAEMU and 13th in West Africa in 2006.

a1179.speaker: Doing Business report 2015 (World Bank)
a1179.speech: Benin was cited as the 2nd best "reformer" in the world, after Tajikistan, recording the strongest progression in the year's ranking among the 189 countries assessed, and progressing since 2012 from 175th place (out of 185) to 151st place (out of 189); according to the 2015 report the business climate has clearly improved in Benin in a good number of areas.

a1179.speaker: International Telecommunication Union (ITU/UIT) (recommendation)
a1179.speech: In 2006, the ITU's recommendation for the transition from analogue to digital from 2015 onwards is an opportunity for the modernisation of broadcasting in Benin.

a1179.speaker: Evaluation of the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) in Benin (report being finalised)
a1179.speech: It emerges from the evaluation that overall the enrolment rates, girl-boy parity and primary completion rates show a very good dynamic; in health, remarkable progress has been made in all the targets, most marked in accessibility to reproductive health care, while progress remains insufficient in infant and maternal mortality and family contraception; in the living environment, the target on accessibility to drinking water has been attained with remarkable progress in basic sanitation.

a1179.speaker: Council of Ministers of Benin (conclusions and recommendations on the energy sector)
a1179.speech: Recommends that, with the effective implementation of the construction of the power plants under the signed power purchase agreements, the period of national emergency for increasing production capacity is no longer to be invoked and new additions of production capacity must now be subject to competitive tendering; it recommends continuing the planning and execution of the main lines of the National Emergency Energy Programme (PEUN), restructuring the sector's companies, agencies and the ministry, adopting a modern Electricity Code, ratifying the Benin-Togo Electricity Code, establishing the energy sector financing fund, putting in place a mechanism and governance to strengthen coordination between the MERPMDER and the MCC, and developing a strategy and action plan to give concrete form to the commitments and benefits of COP21.

a1179.speaker: Agence Francaise de Developpement (AFD)
a1179.speech: After several working sessions and expert missions, AFD has accepted in principle to finance three projects: the installation of computerised management equipment (DMS), the computerisation of SBEE's customer management, and a contribution to the construction of one or more solar power plants with a total capacity of 20 MW with attractive tariffs per kWh.

a1179.speaker: Sinohydro (memorandum of understanding)
a1179.speech: Under the memorandum of understanding, Sinohydro will finance all the feasibility and environmental studies, the creation in Benin of a Centre of Excellence for the maintenance and upkeep of all these thermal and hydroelectric power plants in West Africa, and the computerisation of all the central directorates of the ministry.

a1179.speaker: Government of Benin, through the Ministry of Town Planning, Housing and Sanitation (MUHA)
a1179.speech: In terms of prospects, the government intends to promote the Public-Private Partnership in order to finance the projects of the town planning, housing and sanitation sector and to strengthen the staff of the MUHA by recruiting 199 State agents.

a1219.speaker: Bok Won Kang, South Korea's Ambassador to Mozambique
a1219.speech: "This contribution is dedicated to supporting the people of Mozambique, especially those affected by terrorism and natural disasters in Cabo Delgado," said when announcing the fund in Maputo.

a1219.speaker: International Organisation for Migration (IOM)
a1219.speech: According to the IOM, the fund should contribute to "long-term solutions" and will be used for food security, resilient infrastructure, combating malnutrition, hygiene, providing drinking water, health and protecting children in vulnerable situations.

a1219.speaker: Dinis Zacarias, IOM shelter programme manager
a1219.speech: "The concrete intervention will be in infrastructure and actions based on the needs of the community and it was defined this way to create the greatest level of impact possible."

a1219.speaker: Africa Centre for Strategic Studies (data), academic institution of the US Department of Defence
a1219.speech: According to data recently released, in 2024 alone at least 349 people died in attacks by Islamic extremist groups in the province, an increase of 36% on the previous year.

a1219.speaker: United Nations
a1219.speech: On 27 March, promised to advocate with Mozambique's government to include funding for geospatial technologies in the state budget, as they are important for reducing the impact of natural disasters.

a1219.speaker: Catherine Sozi, United Nations Resident Coordinator in Mozambique
a1219.speech: "We can advocate for United Nations member states to invest in these geospatial technologies (…), we have to continue to raise this issue at the political level so that the [Mozambique's] government commits to funding through the State Budget."

a1219.speaker: United Nations
a1219.speech: Has announced that it needs $222 million (€196 million) this year to assist around 1.4 million Mozambicans affected by the drought associated with the El Niño climate phenomenon, noting that only $41.5 million (€37 million) of this amount, corresponding to 19%, has been disbursed.

a1917.speaker: Britain's National Grid
a1917.speech: said it would pay customers to use less power on Monday and Tuesday evenings this week, the first time it has used a new scheme designed to help prevent power shortages ; said the service would run from 17:00 to 18:00 on Monday, adding that the move did not mean electricity supplies were at risk and advised people not to worry ; said three coal-fired plants had been instructed to warm up to be on standby for Tuesday, and also called on those signed up to the DFS programme to again curb electricity use between 16:30 and 18:00.

a1917.speaker: National Grid
a1917.speech: warned in October that homes could face three-hour rolling power cuts this winter if the country was unable to secure enough gas and electricity imports.

a1917.speaker: Craig Dyke, head of national control at National Grid ESO
a1917.speech: told BBC Radio on Monday that the measures were announced in order to "ensure that everyone gets the electricity they need," adding that 26 suppliers had signed up for the scheme.

a1917.speaker: Met Office (national weather service)
a1917.speech: last week issuing severe weather warnings for snow and ice.

a1917.speaker: National Grid spokesperson (anonymous)
a1917.speech: told Reuters via telephone that a separate measure calling on coal-fired power plants to fire up as back up power was stood down for Monday evening as the supply picture had improved.

a1917.speaker: National Grid ESO (statement)
a1917.speech: The National Grid's ESO said in a statement: [statement text not reproduced in the article].

a1917.speaker: Jonathan Brearley, chief executive of British energy regulator Ofgem
a1917.speech: said on Monday the country's overall power supply outlook had improved from when National Grid first warned of potential power cuts. He said high gas stocks in Europe and an improvement in the operation of French nuclear plants, which often provide electricity to Britain via several power links, had helped to ease the supply risks ; However, "as today's events show ... we need to remain vigilant and cautious about what may happen in the future," he said at an Institute of Government event.

a2039.speaker: General Amara Camara, Spokesperson Minister and Secretary General of the Presidency of the Republic of Guinea
a2039.speech: Assured that President Mamadi Doumbouya is ready "as he has always done" to come to the rescue if necessary: "Our compatriots who need support wherever they are, President Mamadi Doumbouya is ready to bring them help, as he has always done. Wherever Guineans feel threatened and express the need to be assisted by the President, his outstretched hand will be there."

a2039.speaker: General Amara Camara, Secretary General of the Presidency of the Republic of Guinea
a2039.speech: Maintained that relations between the United States and Guinea are excellent and that Guinea is willing to work with the American Administration: "We want to reaffirm here and tell everyone that Guinea maintains excellent relations with the United States. We are doing our best to warm up these relations. We are prepared to work with the American Administration in the interest of our respective countries."

a2100.speaker: Sean Jones, USAID Ethiopia Mission Director
a2100.speech: On his plans: "I believe USAID is here because we have things to offer. America wants friends and partners like Ethiopia. The best ideas, resources and some of our capacity to help Ethiopia through this historic period of time that Ethiopia needs right now. Right now there are many reforms underway that are more focused on democratic values and systems, so our support will be helping Ethiopia in the upcoming election by supporting the election board, we also want to support substantially and the economic reform agenda of the government in line with American values we also need to support the people who need food assistance and humanitarian assistance and crisis response."

a2100.speaker: Sean Jones, USAID Ethiopia Mission Director
a2100.speech: On healthcare: "There is a commitment to stop the spread of HIV. We also want to help alleviate tuberculosis and malaria, we want to continue that, we are not dramatically changing, our level of investment to maintain the gains that Ethiopia has made with HIV in particular, the cases have dropped substantially thanks to the tremendous support and commitment of the Ethiopian government to ensure that the case load is down and identifying new cases very quickly by working with the targeted populations." ; On tuberculosis: "We signed a MOU to continue working with the Ministry of Health. The health system is sufficiently strong now so we are working with civil society organizations."

a2100.speaker: Sean Jones, USAID Ethiopia Mission Director
a2100.speech: On the FITIH justice reform programme: "This program helps protect the rights of citizens and updates the justice system. We are working with the Attorney General and the Ministry of Peace to strengthen the way that it engages with the public to review laws that may need updating and provide additional capacity for Ethiopia's lawyers, judges and prosecutors. It has some focus on capacity building and how to technically implement Ethiopia's vision."

a2100.speaker: Sean Jones, USAID Ethiopia Mission Director
a2100.speech: On the electoral board: "Outside of the National Electoral Board of Ethiopia (NEBE), we are helping civil society organizations and citizens to engage with NEBE to provide advice, on how to conduct free and fair elections." ; On whether the election will be held on schedule: "It is the government's decision but we want to ensure NEBE is as strong as possible for the election. It is a lot of organization, a lot of people, a lot of things have to happen. NEBE is one part of that. The other is the government ensuring security."

a2100.speaker: Sean Jones, USAID Ethiopia Mission Director
a2100.speech: On the private sector and the Jigjiga meat processing plant: "I just have had the opportunity to talk with the general manager, owner and founder of the factory, he closed it temporarily and wants to have another project in that area to grow food for the livestock. Actually he is increasing investment in that area so that he can have a long consistent supply for the factory, that is a tremendous support for the country and I am proud of the investors working in that region investing substantial money. More broadly our investment in the private sector is very important... A robust private sector will do wonders for economic growth." ; "In policy we are working with government officials on reforms to help the private sector. We are working to help businesspeople and farmers to access finance, we are also working with financial institutions so business can access land and resources."

a2100.speaker: Sean Jones, USAID Ethiopia Mission Director
a2100.speech: On agriculture and seeds: "We want to help Ethiopia have less reliance on external factors to grow, produce and sell food while making sure that the crops are healthy." ; "The US government basis this on the needs of the country, not every country desires hybrid seeds, not every country needs genetically modified seeds... we do believe that every country should make their own decisions regarding what types of seeds and technologies and approaches they want to bring to their local market." ; "One is seed varieties. This could be local seeds, weather controlling pests and other pests' like fungus, or it could be the introduction of hybrid seeds that are outside of Ethiopia we work with as well, and when Ethiopia's ready, in a position to have genetically produced seeds or other types of seed technologies we support that, we are not pushing to do that right now we want to have Ethiopian farmers help to have access to seed varieties."

a2100.speaker: Sean Jones, USAID Ethiopia Mission Director
a2100.speech: Rejecting the claim that USAID funds seed shops selling only its own products: "So that is not accurate. I appreciate that because I can help correct it, we went into partnership with a company called Dow DuPont which changed their name to Corteva, what we did is we introduced tens of thousands of farmers to new products that were legally brought by this company and also other companies. We didn't fund them, this is done by the private sector, we encouraged them to use better products." ; On dependency on certain fertilizers: "That is true in general not specific to Corteva, if seed technology has patent rights, and a lot of seed technology doesn't germinate every year, that is true. I think that is farmers' decision whether they can continue or use local seeds even hybrid varieties where they do germinate every year. They can see higher production yield and a higher rate of protection in their farming."

a2100.speaker: Sean Jones, USAID Ethiopia Mission Director
a2100.speech: On economic reform: "This is a new area in our assistance program in Ethiopia, again we are really proud to be invited to provide assistance to the Ministry of Finance, the Prime Minster and the Central Bank. We have brought in a very famous economist and signed a three-year contract and his team from Harvard University to provide advice to the very capable people here the Ethiopian people are leading this reform effort they came and provide assessment, and diagnostics. Particularly it is a critical period for Ethiopia and Ethiopia's economy." ; "They didn't come and start offering advice for them; there are also a bunch of Ethiopian teams that travel here and back to Harvard University in the US. They give advice considering global perspectives, and bring some of the best ideas. It is a conversation between really brilliant people there in Addis Ababa leading reforms and people from Harvard."

a2100.speaker: Sean Jones, USAID Ethiopia Mission Director
a2100.speech: In closing: "We have a lot of projects focused on helping the Ethiopian people one thing about USAID is that we are invited here and we are proud to be a partner of the people and government."

a2357.speaker: US Agency for International Development (USAID) termination letter seen by APA
a2357.speech: Said the termination was done in the "interest of the US government": "This award is being terminated for convenience and the interests of the U.S. Government pursuant to a directive from US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in his capacity as the Acting Administrator for the US Agency for International Development" ; further explained that the decision stemmed from an assessment that continuing these programmes did not align with US national interests.

a2357.speaker: US Agency for International Development (USAID) termination letter seen by APA
a2357.speech: Directed recipients to immediately halt all activities related to their awards and inform any subrecipients or contractors accordingly.

a2363.speaker: Nelson Ramaotwana, Botswana Minister of Justice and Prison Services
a2363.speech: Announced that the rehousing of the rejected asylum seekers would take place soon, during a visit to the Francistown and Dukwi sites, and stressed that it was part of a government policy focused on respect for human dignity, in line with the commitments of President Duma Boko.

a2363.speaker: Nelson Ramaotwana, Botswana Minister of Justice and Prison Services
a2363.speech: Declared: "The term Centre for Illegal Immigrants suggests a place of transit, but it is in reality a prison," while also deploring the systematic separation of families in the centre; explained that children are often separated from their mothers or fathers and placed in the care of adults with no family ties: "Boys without fathers are entrusted to strange men, and girls to women who are not their family."

a2363.speaker: Human rights organisations
a2363.speech: Denounce the prison-like treatment reserved for people in a vulnerable situation, the current policy of prolonged detention having provoked their indignation.

a2457.speaker: Christopher Nyanga, Ministry of Health spokesperson (Botswana)
a2457.speech: Confirmed the cessation of operations at a few agencies, following their initial statement that the United States of America will withdraw from the World Health Organization, which would not affect the availability of ARVs: "There are multiple civil society organisations and non-governmental organisations operating in the health space that were directly affected by the decision to suspend support" ; He added that following this decision most CSOs and NGOs, especially arms performing functions in the HIV/AIDS prevention and treatment, have since closed for business like Tebelopele Voluntary Testing and Counselling centres across the country, "in compliance with the decision".

a2457.speaker: Christopher Nyanga, Ministry of Health spokesperson (Botswana)
a2457.speech: Nyanga assured citizens that despite the recent developments, government would still be able to meet the demands of such services.

a2457.speaker: Ministry of Health of Botswana (statement)
a2457.speech: The ministry has since then advised Batswana to opt for public health services as there is uncertainty as to how long this predicament will persist ; "The ministry also wishes to inform the public that all possible efforts will be made to avail lubricants, condoms and other preventive devices at both public and private facilities so that no gap is experienced" ; The ministry highlighted that to mitigate the situation it would ensure that there are ARVs available at post offices despite the discontinued services at the centres.

a2735.speaker: Economic Report on Africa (ERA) 2025, published by the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (ECA)
a2735.speech: Highlights the urgent need to boost the continent’s economic resilience; according to the document, African economic growth should gradually recover to 3.8% in 2025 and 4.1% in 2026, driven by increased private consumption and improved trade ; warns that this growth is still below what is needed to significantly improve living standards and achieve the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), and that the African economy faces significant risks, including global tensions, regional conflicts and more frequent and severe climate shocks.

a2735.speaker: Economic Report on Africa (ERA) 2025 (ECA)
a2735.speech: Highlights the need to reform the global financial architecture, since high borrowing costs limit the region’s economic growth, noting that despite a reduction in the debt-to-GDP ratio from 67.3% in 2023 to 62.1% in 2025, debt levels remain high, hampering investments essential for development.

a2735.speaker: Economic Report on Africa (ERA) 2025 (ECA)
a2735.speech: Reports that although the extreme poverty rate in Africa is falling, the total number of people living in poverty rose to 468 million, aggravated by recent crises, and that the lack of opportunities for the 76 million African young people without employment, education or training represents a critical challenge; emphasises that investing in skills development is essential for the continent’s sustainable growth.

a2735.speaker: Economic Report on Africa (ERA) 2025 (ECA)
a2735.speech: Warns of the impacts of climate change, which affected more than 110 million people in 2022 and caused economic losses of more than 8.5 billion dollars; the ECA recommends that African countries accelerate climate action to strengthen economic resilience.

a2735.speaker: Economic Report on Africa (ERA) 2025 (ECA)
a2735.speech: Points to the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) as a key factor in reducing external dependence and strengthening self-sufficiency and intra-regional trade, noting that with growing instability in global trade relations, the AfCFTA can offer new opportunities for the continent’s sustainable growth.

a2809.speaker: Population data / statistics
a2809.speech: Population data show that Ethiopia is a country of more than 130 million people, of whom more than 70% are youths below the age of thirty; statistics show that Ethiopia is also one of the biggest economies in Africa and a country that is growing fast.

a2809.speaker: Academics and researchers in politics and economics, including international financial institutions and think tanks
a2809.speech: have confirmed and testified that Ethiopia's march toward a bigger and stronger economy is relentless and unstoppable.

a2809.speaker: Economists
a2809.speech: say that a country without access to the sea would see its economic growth constrained by up to forty percent ; have also noted that if Ethiopia does not have access to the sea, there will be many and unpredictable repercussions, including potentially dangerous scenarios, such as an explosion of hopeless unemployed youths susceptible to being recruited for criminal purposes such as terrorism, human trafficking, and even drug trafficking.

a2960.speaker: Committee of Nigeria's House of Representatives (letter seen by Reuters)
a2960.speech: Sent letters to groups involved in human rights and accountability work, including Transparency International Nigeria, informing them of the probe “with a view to unravelling their real identities, sources of funding and what they expend their monies on”, and demanded they submit audited tax and financial statements, their funding sources, and how they spent their money between 2015 and 2024, within a week; the letter said the investigation was a response to comments made last month by US Congressman Scott Perry.

a2960.speaker: Scott Perry, US Congressman
a2960.speech: Without providing evidence, said USAID had funnelled money to various Islamist groups worldwide, including Boko Haram in Nigeria.

a2960.speaker: Richard Mills, US ambassador to Nigeria
a2960.speech: Rejected Perry's assertion regarding Boko Haram.

a2960.speaker: Auwal Musa Rafsanjani, head of Transparency International in Nigeria
a2960.speech: “On the basis of hearsay, just an unfounded allegation and lack of any proven evidence from either Nigerian security or Nigerian financial agencies, the national assembly will embark on this walk,” he told Reuters.

a2960.speaker: Abiodun Baiyewu, executive director of Global Rights
a2960.speech: Said of the investigation: “It is a brazen attempt at bullying the non-profit sector and not done in good faith.”

a2960.speaker: House of Representatives spokesperson (Nigeria)
a2960.speech: Did not respond to a request for comment on the matter.

a3558.speaker: New York Times electoral model
a3558.speech: According to the New York Times’ electoral model, the probability of victory leans more towards Donald Trump.

a3558.speaker: Rural breeders in Santiago
a3558.speech: Consider the theft of animals a “plague”, facing a distressing reality because they depend on every head of cattle for their livelihood.

a3558.speaker: Main representatives of the Justice system (speeches at the Solemn Session for the Opening of the Judicial Year)
a3558.speech: Reaffirmed their commitment to this fundamental dimension of society and of democracy, acknowledged significant advances, and highlighted the need for robust investment, the urgency of making the sector more agile, as well as the idea that Justice is a collective responsibility that must be accompanied by a “culture of results”.

a3558.speaker: José Ulisses Correia e Silva, Cabo Verdean Prime Minister (speech at the opening of Ocean Week)
a3558.speech: Placed the ocean at the centre of national development.

a3616.speaker: Muhammad Pate, Nigeria’s Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare
a3616.speech: Called for a new vision for global health that places Africa at the core of future governance, trade, financing and innovation, challenging existing frameworks that reduced global health to a narrow set of diseases or priorities largely shaped by external narratives; he said global health is often described through the lens of a few priority issues, like HIV, malaria and tuberculosis, or through specific areas such as health financing or maternal and child health: “Yet these issues are framed by externally driven perspectives, leaving African voices, especially from poorer countries, less acknowledged.”

a3616.speaker: Muhammad Pate, Nigeria’s Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare
a3616.speech: Explained that most health progress in lower-income countries over the past 25 years has depended on domestic financing and local leadership, with donor support playing a complementary role, and warned that shifting geopolitics and nationalist tendencies demand a recalibration: “We cannot build healthier populations purely on the generosity of other nations. It is time to define our path, rooted in sovereignty and aligned with local needs.”

a3616.speaker: Muhammad Pate, Nigeria’s Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare
a3616.speech: Traced the evolution of global health to two contrasting legacies: “The first is the positive legacy of 19th-century international sanitary cooperation, which laid the foundation for today’s collaborative institutions. The second is the colonial legacy, rooted in tropical medicine and neo-colonial economic structures, issues that were powerfully critiqued by Ghana’s Kwame Nkrumah.” He noted the continuity of structural inequities, despite efforts ranging from the Bandung Conference in 1955 and the Alma-Ata Declaration of 1978, to global debt initiatives and public health commissions.

a3616.speaker: Muhammad Pate, Nigeria’s Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare
a3616.speech: Said donor-driven priorities routinely undermine national agency and compromise the independence of institutions like the WHO: “Too often, macroeconomic metrics prioritise short-term ‘value for money’ over the critical public health investments our people need, such as sanitation, clean water, waste management and nutrition.” He warned of fragmentation and dwindling resources despite these structural flaws and the emergence of over 70 global health partnerships like the Global Fund, Gavi and CEPI.

a3616.speaker: Muhammad Pate, Nigeria’s Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare
a3616.speech: “To reclaim leadership in global health, we must act decisively through a seven-point strategic framework” — said the region must forge a strategic South-South alliance uniting Africa, Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean to form a new geopolitical axis committed to equity-driven governance; that it is essential to revise trade terms restricting manufacturing capacity and limiting access to essential medicines; that the continent must champion true country ownership and accountability; “We must push for a more independent and effective WHO by restructuring its funding model to emphasise predictable, unearmarked contributions that allow for impartial and equitable leadership. We need to prioritise domestic financing models. This includes exploring innovative instruments such as pooled regional health funds, diaspora bonds, and blended finance approaches that reduce overreliance on foreign aid.” He said it is important to industrialise the health trade under the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA): “This means engaging trade and finance ministries to build infrastructure for continental markets, harmonise professional standards, and support the health value chain, from diagnostics and test kits to digital health platforms. Finally, we need to strengthen intellectual property protections while encouraging local innovation.”

a3616.speaker: News Agency of Nigeria (NAN)
a3616.speech: Reports that Mr Pate’s vision aligns with broader continental priorities focused on health resilience, economic sovereignty, and inclusive growth, a strategic roadmap emerging from recent high-level African summits.

a3639.speaker: Dr Mohammed Amin Adam, Minister of Finance of Ghana (speech read on his behalf)
a3639.speech: Emphasised the need for the collective responsibility of all stakeholders to ensure the success of Small and Medium-sized Enterprises (SMEs) in Ghana; said SMEs are the lifeblood of the country's economy and therefore the need to create an enabling environment for SMEs to thrive; said that through the SME GO programme the Ministry would bind the public and private sectors together to create a better ecosystem for SMEs.

a3639.speaker: Dr Mohammed Amin Adam, Minister of Finance of Ghana
a3639.speech: Noted that Ghana's growth model must evolve beyond heavy reliance on foreign direct investment and raw material exports, which could be volatile and expose the country to external shocks.

a3639.speaker: Dr Mohammed Amin Adam, Minister of Finance of Ghana
a3639.speech: Said government supported the GEA and GEXIM with a total of 700 million cedis, while Development Bank Ghana committed about 1.2 billion cedis to support SMEs and the International Finance Corporation committed to support SMEs with 400 million dollars through financial institutions.

a3779.speaker: Study by Kamuzu University of Health Sciences (Kuhes)
a3779.speech: Found that the majority of public health facilities in Malawi, including Queen Elizabeth Central Hospital (QECH), do not adhere to international guidelines for pharmaceutical storage, which threatens the quality of medicines ; also concluded that despite having the necessary knowledge on proper storage conditions, pharmacy personnel often fail to adhere to good practices due to resource limitations.

a3779.speaker: International pharmaceutical storage guidelines (cited)
a3779.speech: Recommend that the size of a pharmacy should be based on the number of hospital beds, at a rate of one square metre per bed, assuming monthly medicine deliveries, and that if buffer stock is required the space should be increased accordingly.

a3779.speaker: Associate Professor Felix Khuluza, head of the Kuhes pharmacy department
a3779.speech: “The lack of proper pharmacies affects the storage of pharmaceuticals, as the rooms are too small, leading to the modification of several rooms for pharmacies or reliance on Storage-in-a-Box (SiaBs), For instance, QECH does not have a properly constructed pharmacy, resulting in small storage spaces and reliance on at least three SiaBs, which is not ideal. Some products, especially those requiring cold storage, are kept at the Central Medical Stores Trust.” ; He also observed that without these internal arrangements the quality of medicines would be compromised and security challenges would arise, as SiaBs are sometimes located far from the main pharmacies, and said this also causes delays in dispensing pharmaceutical care as personnel must move around the hospital to retrieve products ; He said most medicines require storage temperatures of between 15 and 30 degrees Celsius, with some needing cold storage at 2-6 degrees Celsius, and stressed that all health facilities providing basic healthcare packages should have refrigerators for cold chain products, with district hospitals encouraged to have them for below 20 degrees Celsius storage.

a3779.speaker: Associate Professor Felix Khuluza, head of the Kuhes pharmacy department
a3779.speech: Said the installation of SiaBs in various health facilities began in 2016, with USaid targeting 115 health facilities in the first year; in 2017 the Global Fund provided funds for an additional 95 SiaBs, and in 2018 USaid added 235 more units; currently over 70 percent of public health facilities and most Christian Health Association of Malawi facilities have SiaBs installed.

a3779.speaker: William Mpute, president of the Pharmaceutical Society of Malawi (Phasom)
a3779.speech: Agreed that most of the country’s old hospitals like QECH and Zomba Central did [not] have modern pharmacy designs in their initial plans, adding that they had to improvise just to have the facilities that operate as pharmacies ; pointed out that government and development partners have tried to put up temporary storage facilities to assist in storage but these facilities are difficult to maintain ; “We recommend that the authorities should prioritise building proper modern pharmacies in our old hospitals if plans to build new hospitals are not in the pipeline. For newer hospitals the situation is better and we recommend that pharmacy structures should be equally prioritised as other facilities for future projects as sometimes developers tend to overlook the significance of this important department.”

a3779.speaker: William Mpute, president of the Pharmaceutical Society of Malawi (Phasom)
a3779.speech: Said the current arrangement of having people stand at the window to receive medicine is outdated, and that there is need for proper dispensing rooms where patients can sit down and get their medicines and proper advice from pharmacy professionals.

a3779.speaker: Maziko Matemba, health activist
a3779.speech: Stressed the need for government intervention and support to address the challenges identified: “Malawi must consistently adhere to national and international standards guidelines, as health is a fundamental human right.”

a3779.speaker: Samson Mndolo, Ministry of Health Principal Secretary
a3779.speech: When contacted for comment, said he needed to review the study first.

a3791.speaker: United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) (statement)
a3791.speech: Has warned that millions in Somalia are at risk of worsening hunger and malnutrition amid critical funding shortfalls the agency faces ; said it is forced to reduce the number of people it supports with lifesaving emergency food assistance in Somalia by over two-thirds ; said WFP's nutrition programs are also facing reductions with just 180,000 children still receiving nutrition treatment ; said Somalia's hunger crisis is unfolding in a fragile and fast-moving context, where even the smallest shocks can have devastating consequences for families and communities ; "This year, the compounded effects of severe drought, conflict, and reduced humanitarian assistance have rapidly pushed the most vulnerable families into emergency levels of food insecurity. Without urgent action, this trend is likely to continue, and could tip those worst affected into catastrophic conditions."

a3791.speaker: Ross Smith, WFP's Director of Emergency Preparedness and Response
a3791.speech: "We are seeing a dangerous rise in emergency levels of hunger, and our ability to respond is shrinking by the day." ; "Without urgent funding, families already pushed to the edge will be left with nothing at a time when they need it most." ; warned, "The current level of response is far below what is required to meet the growing needs."

a3791.speaker: Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) report
a3791.speech: Shows that 4.4 million people in Somalia are facing crisis level of food insecurity or worse (IPC 3+), including nearly 1 million in emergency levels of hunger (IPC 4), a number that has increased by 50 percent in just six months.

a3825.speaker: Luis Francisco Martinez Montes, Spanish diplomat
a3825.speech: According to him, Urdaneta’s decision to take to the seas again was a momentous one: starting his trip in 1565 from the Philippines, Urdaneta defied conventional wisdom, heading north towards Japan and then east towards California and Acapulco, completing four months later the first round trip between the Philippines and America and opening the first systematic transoceanic route in human history.

a3825.speaker: Luis Francisco Martinez Montes, Spanish diplomat
a3825.speech: Stated that contrary to the alleged success of the English and Dutch sea-dogs in plundering the Spanish fleets, the historic truth is that throughout the 250 years of its existence, only four Manila Galleons were captured by the enemy — the first the “Santa Ana” in 1587 and the last the “Santisima Trinidad” in 1762 ; further noted that this is a very meagre rate of capture by any measure.

a3825.speaker: Luis Francisco Martínez Montes, Spanish diplomat
a3825.speech: Stated that Pillar dollars with the effigy of Charles IV, of Goya fame, were called the “fatty Budas” ; according to him, more luxurious goods were purchased by the Spanish American elite, or found their way to Spanish and European markets via Seville.

a3825.speaker: Giacomo Mendes Garcia, Spanish historian
a3825.speech: Stated that since the Leyes de Indias forbade the enslavement of native Indians, they had to provide them with a salary, and minimum as this remuneration might be, it was enough to make silk production in America uncompetitive.

a3825.speaker: Giacomo Mendes Garcia, Spanish historian
a3825.speech: Noted that, for the Chinese, the Manila Galleon presented two obvious advantages: first, it provided a regular channel, financed and defended by foreigners, through which it could export part of its excess production to a wider market without incurring the cost of running an overseas empire; second, the Galleon was a source of much needed money in times of financial distress.

a3825.speaker: Alexander von Humboldt, German traveler
a3825.speech: Witnessed in his travels through Spanish America around 1803 that Far Eastern spices and textiles had become part of Indian and mestizo populations’ daily life, thus contributing to a quintessentially Hispanic mixing of habits and customs.

a4103.speaker: Central Bank of Nigeria
a4103.speech: Still trying to steady the naira and tame inflation, has hinted at another interest rate hike.

a4140.speaker: A US official (anonymous)
a4140.speech: Told AFP on Saturday that Egypt and Israel had agreed to let Americans leave the Gaza Strip via Rafah, but that Egypt imposed conditions.

a4140.speaker: Senior sources quoted by media outlets close to the intelligence services (anonymous)
a4140.speech: Said Egypt “refuses to allow the border crossing to be exclusively dedicated to the passage of foreigners” ; “The Egyptian position is clear: the condition (for these crossings) is that the entry of aid into Gaza be facilitated,” they added.

a4140.speaker: Witnesses (unnamed)
a4140.speech: Reported today that the concrete blocks installed by the Egyptians after the Israeli bombardment to reinforce their border were still in place, which seems to indicate that no crossing is planned in the immediate future.

a4140.speaker: Israel (government)
a4140.speech: Declared a “total siege” of the Palestinian territory, after 16 years of blockade, banning the entry of food and cutting off water and electricity to the territory’s 2.4 million inhabitants.

a4140.speaker: Israeli army
a4140.speech: On Friday ordered the 1.1 million inhabitants of the northern Gaza Strip to withdraw to the south, which borders Egypt.

a4172.speaker: Samson Asaaki Awingobit, President of the Importers and Exporters Association of Ghana (IEAG)
a4172.speech: Has expressed his doubts about the possibility of abolishing the electronic transaction levy (e-levy) despite promises from political parties to do so ; noted that both the New Patriotic Party (NPP) and the National Democratic Congress (NDC) supported the passage of the e-levy law, making it unlikely that they will follow through on their promise to abolish it ; believes even though it has significantly hurt importers and exporters, causing them to operate at a loss, the tax will be maintained irrespective of which political party wins power ; was of the opinion that political promises do not always turn to be followed through as the economic realities set in when a new political government assumes power.

a4172.speaker: Samson Asaaki Awingobit, President of the Importers and Exporters Association of Ghana (IEAG)
a4172.speech: Was of the opinion that the next government must rather take a holistic view of all the overall taxes regimes with a view of abolishing nuisances taxes that hurts business ; advised that government’s efforts must aim at driving down the cost of doing business generally in Ghana rather than imposing more taxes ; “Taxes such as COVID levy should scrapped as well other taxes associated with the imports and exports to make the country products especially exports attractive on the international markets.”

a4172.speaker: Samson Asaaki Awingobit, President of the Importers and Exporters Association of Ghana (IEAG)
a4172.speech: After the law's passage, encouraged members of the Import and Export Association to use cheques and cash for payments rather than electronic platforms to avoid incurring electronic transaction taxes.

a4210.speaker: Richard M. Mills, United States Ambassador to Nigeria (opinion article)
a4210.speech: Writes that “The US Embassy stands ready to support Nigerian voices pressing the fight against corruption in Nigeria,” and that “The United States remains your steadfast partner on this journey” ; states that for two decades the United States has stood with Nigeria in the fight against HIV/AIDS under PEPFAR, investing more than $8.3 billion in Nigeria’s health sector and providing life-saving anti-retroviral treatment to more than 1.5 million people ; argues that positive health outcomes depend critically on good governance, that “when medical supplies are diverted, when healthcare workers go unpaid, when facilities buy dangerous, counterfeit medications or lack resources due to mismanaged funds, it costs lives,” and that this is why the United States supports initiatives to enhance transparency and accountability in Nigeria ; concludes that “These three areas – health, transparency, and human rights – reinforce each other” and that “The United States continues to stand with the Nigerian people as they carry out this essential work with their elected government.”

a4210.speaker: Ambassador John Nkengasong (US Global AIDS Coordinator), via reported visit
a4210.speech: His recent visit reinforced the commitment, with discussions with Nigerian health officials focused on how the government of Nigeria would sustain the HIV health programmes with strengthened Nigerian leadership and local ownership.

a4210.speaker: United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (recent survey)
a4210.speech: According to a recent survey by the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, Nigerians are both more frequently refusing to pay bribes and reporting bribe seekers to investigative journalists and rule of law authorities.

a4491.speaker: Experts / economic analysts (unnamed)
a4491.speech: Warn that the US foreign aid freeze could create a substantial funding gap, potentially disrupting ongoing development projects and essential services ; Criticized the government's lack of response, noting that the public expected budget estimates to address the issue and clarify its strategy for mitigating the funding shortfall; analysts mention that the budget estimates might have been finalized before the aid freeze was announced on January 20, but hoped the Minister of Finance should have acknowledged the potential impact and outlined a plan during her speech, and argued that addressing the aid freeze in the budget speech would have demonstrated the government's commitment to managing the economic challenges it poses.

a4491.speaker: Dr Retselisitsoe Matlanyane, Minister of Finance and Development Planning of Lesotho
a4491.speech: Underscored the urgency of addressing youth unemployment, citing the 2024 Labour Force Survey: "Among the 760 230 young Basotho aged 15 to 35, approximately 145 087 are currently unemployed. This figure is striking; nearly 39 percent of our youth actively looking for work are unable to secure a job." ; Emphasized that these statistics represent more than just numbers - they reflect deferred dreams and unfulfilled potential ; Noted that opportunities exist in the informal sector, which currently employs 461 873 people, compared to 87 849 in the formal sector, and urged the private sector to play a leading role in expanding job creation, particularly in emerging economic sectors.

a4491.speaker: 2024 Labour Force Survey (Lesotho)
a4491.speech: Cited by the Minister of Finance as the source for the figures that among the 760 230 young Basotho aged 15 to 35, approximately 145 087 are currently unemployed.

a4491.speaker: Many citizens (unnamed)
a4491.speech: Many citizens saying that the Ministry of Health is vital to ensuring the well-being of citizens, thus a reduction of M0.3 billion may seem minor, but it could significantly impact the ministry's ability to provide quality healthcare, especially if the aid freeze is not adequately addressed.

a4491.speaker: Dr Retselisitsoe Matlanyane, Minister of Finance and Development Planning of Lesotho
a4491.speech: On the health budget: maintained that the allocated funds would support the Ministry of Health in delivering essential services: "As we continue to grapple with the burden of both communicable and non-communicable diseases, we are committed to taking bold steps to enhance health services and innovation across the nation." ; "This approach will help reduce the incidence of diseases such as tuberculosis (TB), HIV/Aids, and chronic non-communicable conditions like hypertension and diabetes, while also strengthening our healthcare infrastructure." ; "In our fight against tuberculosis, we are employing innovative tools such as digital X-ray technology with Artificial Intelligence (AI) to improve diagnostic accuracy and advance our healthcare sector." ; She noted that integrating health services with local community systems and supporting healthcare workers would enhance health security, biosecurity, and patient safety, and added that the government remains committed to tackling HIV/Aids through comprehensive testing, treatment, and prevention initiatives to ensure no one is left behind.

a4491.speaker: Remaketse Sehlabaka, Member of Parliament and leader of the Mpulule Political Summit
a4491.speech: Condemned the government's handling of both the aid freeze and the reduced health budget: "The budget estimates fail to address this crucial issue, raising questions about the government's competence and commitment to protecting economic stability. These are not matters that can be ignored." ; She further warned that every day without a clear plan from the government increases uncertainty for citizens and the economy ; However, she noted that since the budget estimates are still subject to review and debate in parliamentary committees, legislators would use the opportunity to push for clarity on the government's approach to handling the aid freeze and the reduced health budget.

a4491.speaker: Dr Retselisitsoe Matlanyane, Minister of Finance and Development Planning of Lesotho
a4491.speech: On old-age pensions: defended the government's decision not to increase pensions, explaining that pensioners had received increases in the past two years, while grants for orphans, vulnerable children, and people with disabilities had remained unchanged: "When we increased the grants for elderly people in previous years, those with disabilities did not complain." ; "However, these vulnerable groups, especially disabled individuals and orphans, face severe conditions." ; "These children need diapers and various other necessities, yet they receive only M250 per month. Meanwhile, elderly people receive M950 per month and still complain when we allocate just M50 more to those with disabilities and other vulnerable groups." ; "As a community, we need to recognize why certain decisions are made. Consider the gap between M250 and M950 and the conditions in which these groups live before criticizing the adjustments."

a4513.speaker: Malawi Economic Justice Network (Mejn)
a4513.speech: Says declining social protection spending can exacerbate poverty, widen inequality and increase social unrest.

a4513.speaker: Bertha Phiri, Mejn executive director
a4513.speech: Said in a written response on Tuesday that to avert the situation, there is need to diversify the economy and ensure that income generating sectors are supported to increase domestic revenue mobilisation ; "The vulnerable populations may struggle to access essential services such as healthcare and education. Lower social spending can also widen income inequality, potentially leading to social unrest and decreased economic growth."

a4513.speaker: Malawi 2025 Commitment to Reducing Inequality Profile (published data)
a4513.speech: Indicates that Malawi's social protection spending is low, dropping from 5.7 percent to 2.3 percent of the National Budget within two years, ranking among the lowest in Southern Africa; according to the profile, most funds go to civil service pensions, covering less than three percent of older people, while child benefits have broader coverage with the social cash transfer programme reaching about 300 000 households, but 97 percent is donor support, now at risk due to aid cuts.

a4513.speaker: Ministry of Finance and Economic Affairs (data)
a4513.speech: Data show that out of the K8.07 trillion 2025/26 National Budget, social benefits now stand at K286 billion, a decline from the K378 billion in 2024/25 fiscal year revised estimates, with K4.4 billion channelled towards the Social Cash Transfer Programme.

a4513.speaker: Bond Mtembezeka, Business Partners International country manager
a4513.speech: Observed in an interview on Tuesday that ordinarily, a decline in social expenditure should be a result of improved economic welfare in the sense that those that were previously aided have graduated into a better level of economic welfare warranting such a reduction ; "However in the local context, with how poverty levels have grown over the last few years, it signals that government has cut such expenditure due to most likely fiscal pressures. We have a situation where poverty levels are growing and social expenditure is declining and the effects are deterioration in welfare."

a4513.speaker: Agness Nyirongo, Centre for Social Concern economic governance officer
a4513.speech: Observed that underfunding social protection will leave millions of Malawians vulnerable and stifle the country's economic potential as investments in the sectors critical for reducing poverty and inequality are being sacrificed to repay debts, leaving ordinary Malawians more vulnerable ; "Failure to act now risks locking another generation in poverty, but with bold policy choices, prioritising people over debt, raising more domestic revenue fairly and investing in inclusive social programmes, Malawi can unlock the potential of its youth, reduce inequality and move closer to its development vision."

a4513.speaker: World Bank (data)
a4513.speech: Data show that following the upward revision of the international poverty line (IPL) for low-income countries, including Malawi, to $3 (about K5 253) per person per day, Malawi's poverty rate now stands at 75.4 percent; under the previous IPL of $2.15 (about K3 764) per person per day, the poverty rate using the same data was at 70.1 percent, according to the bank.

a4671.speaker: Alexis Lamek, French Ambassador to Ethiopia
a4671.speech: Said France's recognition of Palestinian statehood is part of an effort to further strengthen and energise the role of multilateral forums in the face of the terrible wars seen at the international level; in a briefing to journalists said that standing on the sidelines and waiting over the Gaza crisis would only worsen the crisis, and that countries extending recognition, as part of the solution, is taken as a major option for peace; explained that many resolutions are repeatedly tabled at the UN Security Council to resolve world crises but have not been able to stop the wars; noted that at the UN high-level international conference held in New York on July 29, 2025, a resolution centred on Israel and Palestine becoming two states was adopted, led by France and Saudi Arabia; explained that the two-state solution France launched is one key way by which the standing of the multilateral forum is improved and revitalised.

a4671.speaker: Alexis Lamek, French Ambassador to Ethiopia
a4671.speech: Said the crisis between Israel and Hamas cannot be resolved by condemnation alone; said France believes peace in the region benefits everyone and that, because his country is committed to peace, this terrible situation must stop; said that although the diplomatic effort is difficult, doing nothing is not an option given the war's current state: “We have the determination that we must move forward.” ; said that in granting statehood recognition to Palestine they do so out of a commitment that Hamas should have no political role whatsoever, either in Gaza or on Palestinian soil, and to create a way for the Israeli hostages to be released.

a4671.speaker: Alexis Lamek, French Ambassador to Ethiopia
a4671.speech: Explained that the decision on Palestinian statehood is based on the 1967 border agreement, and said the annexation talk by Israeli officials following the recognition is “our red line” ; “The statement by Israeli officials is an unhelpful decision”, and because it departs from the wishes not only of Palestinians but also of Israelis: “What we are saying is that recognition of two states is an opportunity for both to live in peace. It is for the international community to make every effort expected of it.”

a4846.speaker: Donald Trump, US President (executive order of 20 January)
a4846.speech: Issued an executive order suspending almost all foreign aid programmes for 90 days, now in effect in Mozambique, with the sole exemptions being emergency food aid and military aid to Israel and Egypt.

a4846.speaker: United States Agency for International Development (USAID), local branch in Mozambique
a4846.speech: Immediately ordered a halt to all the projects it is financing.

a4846.speaker: "Carta de Moçambique" (independent newssheet)
a4846.speech: According to it, total investment by USAID in Mozambique is running at over a billion US dollars a year, of which 400 million dollars a year is spent on programmes to fight HIV/AIDS.

a4846.speaker: Peter Vrooman, US ambassador to Mozambique (in 2022)
a4846.speech: Claimed "solidarity between the American people and the Mozambican people has allowed us to reduce by almost half the number of deaths from HIV/AIDS. We are financing humanitarian assistance to the displaced people in Cabo Delgado" ; pointed out that the US "is the largest donor of vaccines against Covid-19 through the Covax initiative of the international community".

a4873.speaker: United Nations Security Council (resolution adopted Monday)
a4873.speech: Adopted a resolution demanding an immediate ceasefire in Gaza during the month of Ramadan, the immediate and unconditional release of all hostages, and stressing the urgent need to "expand the flow" of aid into the Palestinian enclave; the resolution "demands an immediate humanitarian ceasefire during the month of Ramadan that is respected by all parties and leads to a lasting ceasefire" ; "also demands the immediate and unconditional release of all hostages and the guarantee of humanitarian access to address their medical and other humanitarian needs, and further demands that the parties comply with their obligations under international law in relation to all persons they detain."

a4873.speaker: United Nations Security Council members (resolution text)
a4873.speech: The members of the Security Council declare themselves "deeply concerned about the catastrophic humanitarian situation prevailing in the Gaza Strip" and take note of the ongoing diplomatic action led by Egypt, the United States and Qatar, "aimed at achieving a cessation of hostilities, obtaining the release of the hostages and increasing the provision and distribution of humanitarian aid"; they insist "on the urgent need to expand the delivery of humanitarian aid to civilians and to strengthen the protection of civilians throughout the Gaza Strip" and "again demand the lifting of all obstacles to the provision of large-scale humanitarian aid."

a4873.speaker: UN News (ONU Info) (cited source)
a4873.speech: Cited as the source of the report: "Source: ONU Info."

a5199.speaker: Aaron Motsoaledi, South African Health Minister
a5199.speech: At a press conference last week gave a public tongue-lashing to the media, activists and researchers, accusing them of making an “AfriForum-style” scene to “spread disinformation” ; says activists are effectively lying because US government funding comprises only 17% of the country's HIV budget of R46 billion ; “I want to state it clearly that propagating wrong information about the start of the HIV and Aids campaign in South Africa, in the matter that it is being done, is no different from the approach adopted by AfriForum and its ilk which led Trump to trash the whole country” ; “I am saying so because we have already been phoned by the funders we have spoken to, who are asking us, why should they put their money in the programme that is said to be collapsing. Is their money going to collapse together with the programme?”

a5199.speaker: Aaron Motsoaledi, South African Health Minister
a5199.speech: Explained at the press conference that of 63,322 clients served by the 12 Pepfar-funded clinics with tailor-made HIV services for key populations, 41,996 — two-thirds — live in Johannesburg ; says all the patients' files have been transferred to the nearest government facility ; says 1,012 clinicians and 2,377 non-clinician workers at government health facilities, most of them in Gauteng, are being trained to make key populations feel more comfortable to visit state clinics for HIV services.

a5199.speaker: Aaron Motsoaledi, South African Health Minister
a5199.speech: Announced at his press conference that the health department has made progress with getting people with HIV who stopped treatment back onto their pills, and that government health workers have managed to find close to half — 520,700 — of the 1.1 million people with HIV that they've been looking for and put them on treatment ; said South Africa is at 96-79-94 on the 95-95-95 targets, which means the country is struggling to get people who know they've got HIV onto treatment, or to prevent people who are on treatment from defaulting on drugs.

a5199.speaker: Fatima Hassan, lawyer and head of the Health Justice Initiative
a5199.speech: “The minister is in denial that there's a crisis at all. We have been here before. No amount of finger pointing will save lives — only urgency, evidence, partnership, proper planning and resources will” ; “Once again, South Africa will have to deal with the harmful public health consequences of not just the Trump administration, but also our own government's failure to adequately plan for months now.”

a5199.speaker: Kate Rees, public health specialist at the Anova Health Institute
a5199.speech: Says the US government is allowing Anova to keep only two of its mobile clinics and even those they can't use because they no longer have money for staff to run them ; says the stop-work order is already being felt in the data — March 2025 health department figures show that 30% fewer people took up ART in the City of Johannesburg than in March 2024.

a5199.speaker: Kate Rees, public health specialist at the Anova Health Institute
a5199.speech: Says the minister's numbers are incredibly misleading: “The minister didn't subtract the number of people who were lost from care — those who stopped treatment or died — from the people with HIV who started or restarted treatment. If that was the number we were interested in, we would have reached our targets years ago” ; says that's part of the reason why South Africa's total number of people on ART has been lingering between 5.7 and 5.9 million for the past two years ; “Because of people who fall off treatment, we're seeing static programme growth. So we're not seeing significant increases in the number of people on treatment overall. That means that although the 500 000 people they say they've now put onto treatment may have been added to the treatment group, another 500 000 who had already been on treatment could very well also have stopped their treatment during this time. In many cases, it's possibly the same people cycling in and out of treatment.”

a5199.speaker: Patients transferred from closed Pepfar-funded clinics
a5199.speech: Many have told Bhekisisa they've been refused services — often because government nurses tell them they don't have transfer letters or they “don't deserve to be helped”.

a5199.speaker: Treatment Action Campaign (HIV advocacy organisation) and Sisonke (national sex worker movement)
a5199.speech: Confirmed many more such experiences on a webinar hosted last week by Bhekisisa and the Southern African HIV Clinicians Society.

a5199.speaker: Thatho Chidarikire, former acting head of HIV in the South African health department
a5199.speech: Told Bhekisisa's TV programme, Health Beat, in May 2023 that the health department has in fact been busy with such training for years.

a5199.speaker: Surveys by the Ritshidze group
a5199.speech: Have shown that severe discrimination against transgender people and sex workers persists.

a5199.speaker: A sex worker (anonymous), pregnant and fearful of transmitting the virus to her child
a5199.speech: “I have defaulted on my ART for two months now. I have tried to go to a public clinic, but I wasn't helped. Sex workers are seen as dirty people who go and sleep around. We even struggle to get condoms. People like me are now forced to do business without protection because it's our only source of income and it's the way we put food on the table.”

a5199.speaker: Modelling study commissioned by the health minister
a5199.speech: Shows that if South Africa fails to replace the Pepfar funds the country has lost, we might see between 150,000 and 295,000 extra new HIV infections over the next four years (in addition to the estimated 130,000 new infections we already have each year) and up to a 38% increase in Aids-related deaths.

a5199.speaker: Nicholas Crisp, deputy director general in the national health department
a5199.speech: Told Bhekisisa in April that, with Pepfar data, the health department calculated it needs an extra R2.82 billion to get through the financial year, and that without replacement funds South Africa's HIV programme would be “unsustainable.”

a5199.speaker: Francois Venter, head of Ezintsha and HIV scientist
a5199.speech: Describes the health department's reported progress in getting people with HIV who stopped treatment back onto their pills as “inconceivable.”

a5199.speaker: Linda-Gail Bekker, HIV scientist, head of the Desmond Tutu Health Foundation
a5199.speech: “We saw amazing leadership during Covid. [Because of the leadership], private funding followed. But we're not seeing it this time around. My concern is it doesn't feel like anyone [in the health department] is in charge” ; “We need to all put our minds together in a room and work out what are our best buys and how do we get those out to people who need it the most. The government can't solve this problem on its own.”

a5199.speaker: Foster Mohale, South African health department spokesperson
a5199.speech: Says interviews for the deputy director general position for HIV and TB, vacant for five years, only started in the past few months.

a5199.speaker: Office of Ramphelane Morewane, acting deputy director general
a5199.speech: Told Bhekisisa he was on leave in the days prior to the 8 May webinar, but “would definitely be there” — though Morewane didn't turn up, no one was sent in his place, and no one explained why the health department couldn't make it.

a5199.speaker: Ndiviwe Mphothulo, head of the Southern African HIV Clinicians Society
a5199.speech: “History tells us the reason our ART programmes have been so successful is because the government worked with civil society. People who won't learn from history, repeat the mistakes from history.”

a5199.speaker: A young transwoman in Hillbrow (anonymous)
a5199.speech: “I'm anxious and depressed, each day. At the Wits clinic, I got my treatment without being made fun of and I got self-testing kits for my sexual partners. But, most importantly, I could get mental health for free” ; “My friends visited the government Hillbrow clinic the other day. I couldn't even get condoms, let alone treatment.”

a5280.speaker: Zhongshan Fucheng Industrial Investment Co. Limited and its parent company
a5280.speech: Accused the Ogun State government of terminating its contract before it had reached fruition, in a case arising from an export-free-zone business deal entered into with the Ogun government 17 years ago.

a5280.speaker: The governors involved in the saga
a5280.speech: Have the audacity to ask the federal government not to give in to the firm's judgment debt.

a5280.speaker: The Internet ("the usually unreliable Internet")
a5280.speech: According to the usually unreliable Internet, depending on the specs of an Escalade, the price ranges between $80,000 to $150,000.

a5300.speaker: Elia Kaiyamo, Namibia's Ambassador to China
a5300.speech: "Of late, private investors have shown increased interest in various economic sectors other than the traditional extractive investments in projects such as Green Hydrogen development" ; the recent wave of investor interests in the country includes a promising mix of private equity, venture capital, and other asset classes, which could be directed towards infrastructure, commercial real estate and technical development.

a5300.speaker: Elia Kaiyamo, Namibia's Ambassador to China
a5300.speech: noted that in terms of bilateral trade in 2019, the total volume between China and Namibia was about US$709 million, with a year-on-year decrease in 2018 of 14.28% from US$800 million. "Obviously, the pandemic has adversely affected these numbers in 2020 and this year" ; added Chinese companies have contributed N$250 million in tax revenue to the Namibian government since 2016, while creating up to 11 000 direct and indirect jobs in the country.

a5300.speaker: Elia Kaiyamo, Namibia's Ambassador to China
a5300.speech: "Another achievement is that Namibia in 2018 became one of the first African countries allowed by the Chinese authorities to export beef to China. With that, the first consignment of prime Namibian beef was delivered to China in 2019".

a5300.speaker: Elia Kaiyamo, Namibia's Ambassador to China
a5300.speech: noted that China, in particular, has been supporting Namibia's economic and social development and offering development assistance in many projects over the years, including the construction of national buildings, hospitals, clinics, schools, roads and port infrastructure ; pointed out that China has assisted Namibia with aid of various forms that have helped to improve people's living standards, many of these projects a result of Namibia's participation in FOCAC.

a5300.speaker: Elia Kaiyamo, Namibia's Ambassador to China
a5300.speech: "Namibia also benefits under the Belt and Road Initiative of China where eight areas of cooperation were identified. Namibia will take full advantage of the traditional friendship, consolidate our all-weather friendship, deepen pragmatic cooperation and enrich and expand channels of communication between the two friendly nations, and promote the strategic development of bilateral relations."

a5300.speaker: Elia Kaiyamo, Namibia's Ambassador to China
a5300.speech: informed Forum participants of Namibia's abundance of natural resources, consisting of a wide range of mineral deposits, including world-class diamonds and uranium, copper, lead, zinc, gold, semi-precious stones, industrial minerals, salt and fluorspar. "Our rich fishing grounds are well known across the world in the international fishing industry" ; "Such valuable resources mean mining and fishing are two of our most important economic sectors, together with agriculture, including a thriving red meat industry and tourism. Tourism, indeed, is a rapidly growing sector, and it is fast becoming a major earner of foreign exchange and generator of income for the nation. Our infrastructure is superior to that found in many places in Africa and other parts of the world. We have an excellent road and rail network, including trans-continental links to the Atlantic seaport of Walvis Bay, which, with its world-class standard of cargo handling and sheltered deep-water harbour, is poised to grow into the most important port on Africa's west coast and a regional container hub for southern Africa".

a5300.speaker: Elia Kaiyamo, Namibia's Ambassador to China
a5300.speech: said there are two important and excellent cooperation achievements in Namibia, to which few other African countries can make comparisons - space science cooperation and the space tracking station in Swakopmund: "In 2018, during his state visit to China, our President Geingob visited the Beijing Aerospace Control Center and interacted with Chinese astronauts. He invited the astronauts to Namibia. In 2019, Yang, China's first female astronaut in space, and her colleague Dong, arrived in Namibia's port town of Walvis Bay; the visit was aimed at enhancing communication and cooperation on astronautics between China and Namibia" ; "The tracking station has been in operation since 2000, and it is a symbol of scientific and technological cooperation linking Namibia and China together for the peaceful use of space".

a5386.speaker: António Guterres, UN Secretary-General
a5386.speech: says Sudan is on the brink of a “full-scale civil war”.

a5386.speaker: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
a5386.speech: According to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, more than 2.8 million people have been displaced by the war, including more than 2.2 million inside the country and nearly 615 000 who have crossed the border into neighbouring countries.

a5386.speaker: Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD) (communiqué)
a5386.speech: called on “states neighbouring the Republic of Sudan to step up efforts for the delivery of humanitarian assistance and to take necessary measures to ease and lift any logistical barriers to the delivery of humanitarian aid, including visa and customs requirements” ; “The IGAD further resolves to request the Eastern Africa Standby Force (EASF) summit to convene to consider the possible deployment of the EASF for the protection of civilians and guarantee of humanitarian access.”

a5386.speaker: Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD) (communiqué)
